question: Is higher density always the more sustainable choice for a growing city? Make the case against it.
lookingFor: Ability to hold a position while genuinely arguing the other side, showing density isn't a slogan but a trade-off.

bullets: Acknowledge density's real benefits: shorter trips, cheaper infrastructure per capita, transit viability
Give a genuine counter-argument: infrastructure strain, loss of green space per resident, resistance from existing communities, or heat island effects if not paired with design quality
Land on a nuanced position rather than a flat yes or no
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Density is usually the more efficient answer because it shortens trips and makes public transit and shared infrastructure viable in a way sprawl never can. But I don't think it's automatically sustainable. If you densify without upgrading sewage, schools, or green space at the same pace, you just concentrate the strain instead of solving it, and you can get worse heat island effects and overcrowded amenities. I'd argue density is sustainable when it's matched with infrastructure investment and genuine mixed-income access, not just taller buildings on the same old grid.

commonMistakes: Treating density as an unqualified good with no downside
Confusing density with height, ignoring low-rise high-density models
Giving a one-word answer without reasoning through the trade-off
followUps: Can you name a city that got density wrong, and why?

question: Explain what single-family zoning is and why it has become such a contested policy in North American planning debates.
lookingFor: Solid grasp of the concept plus awareness of the housing-affordability and equity debate around it.

bullets: Define single-family zoning correctly: land reserved exclusively for detached one-unit housing
Explain the critique: it restricts housing supply, drives up prices, and has a documented history tied to exclusion
Note the counter-argument from residents defending neighbourhood character and property values
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Single-family zoning restricts a parcel of land to one detached house, which sounds neutral but has huge downstream effects, because it locks out duplexes, triplexes, and apartments from most of a city's land area. Critics argue it's a major driver of housing shortages and, historically, was used alongside redlining to keep neighbourhoods economically and racially exclusive. The pushback against upzoning it comes from residents worried about parking, infrastructure capacity, and neighbourhood character, and I think that resistance is genuine even where the underlying policy needs reform, which is why cities like Minneapolis phasing it out slowly rather than overnight makes sense to me.

commonMistakes: Defining the term but never engaging with why it's controversial
Dismissing residents' concerns as purely selfish with no acknowledgment of legitimate infrastructure worries
Confusing single-family zoning with historic preservation zoning
followUps: How would you sequence an upzoning to minimise backlash?

question: A council wants to redevelop a rundown but affordable neighbourhood into a mixed-use district that will raise property values and likely displace long-term low-income residents. As the planner advising them, what do you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that treats displacement as a real cost to weigh, not an inconvenient footnote to progress.

bullets: Name the tension honestly: improved infrastructure and investment versus displacement of the people already there
Propose concrete mitigations: anti-displacement zoning, right-to-return policies, phased development, community land trusts, or inclusionary requirements
Show you'd prioritise resident input over simply proceeding on the council's timeline
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't treat this as redevelopment versus no redevelopment, because that framing lets the real question slide, which is who benefits and who pays. I'd push the council to build in protections before breaking ground: rent stabilisation for existing tenants, a right-to-return clause for anyone displaced during construction, and a requirement that a real share of new units stay affordable long-term, maybe through a community land trust. And I'd want genuine resident consultation, not a single public meeting used to check a box, because the people who'll live with the consequences should shape the plan, not just react to it.

commonMistakes: Treating displacement as an unavoidable and acceptable side effect of progress
Refusing any development at all, avoiding the actual dilemma
Proposing consultation as a formality rather than something that changes the plan
followUps: What if the council rejects your mitigations to save budget? What do you do then?

question: What do you understand by the '15-minute city' concept, and why has it attracted both praise and conspiracy-driven backlash?
lookingFor: Accurate grasp of the concept plus awareness of the real public discourse and misinformation around it.

bullets: Define it correctly: daily needs (work, shops, school, healthcare, leisure) reachable within a 15-minute walk or cycle
Note genuine benefits argued for it: less car dependence, stronger local economies, lower emissions
Show awareness that it has been misrepresented in some places as a plot to restrict movement, and explain why that framing is inaccurate but still shapes public reaction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The idea, associated with Carlos Moreno's work on Paris, is that most of what someone needs day to day should be within a short walk or cycle ride, so the city works at a human scale rather than forcing car trips for basic errands. I think the appeal is real: it cuts emissions, supports local shops, and gives people time back. What surprised me was the backlash in places like Oxford, where some residents genuinely believed it was about restricting where people are allowed to travel, which isn't what the policy proposes at all. It taught me that even a sound planning idea needs a communication strategy, because misinformation can undo good policy just as easily as bad design can.

commonMistakes: Confusing the concept with traffic restriction zones or congestion charging
Being unaware of the public controversy entirely
Dismissing the backlash without acknowledging why it gained traction
followUps: How would you communicate a 15-minute city plan to avoid that kind of backlash?

question: Should a city be allowed to use eminent domain to seize private property for a project that primarily benefits a private developer, even if it creates jobs and tax revenue?
lookingFor: Ability to reason through a genuinely contested legal and ethical question rather than reciting a textbook definition.

bullets: Show understanding of what eminent domain is and the 'public use' justification debate, referencing the Kelo v. New London controversy if relevant
Weigh the public-benefit argument against the property-rights and equity concerns, including who typically loses these fights
Reach a reasoned position, ideally with conditions rather than an absolute yes or no
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know this is exactly what the Kelo case tested in the US, where the court allowed a city to take homes for private economic development, and it's stayed controversial ever since. My instinct is that eminent domain for private benefit should be a last resort, not a shortcut, because the people who lose their homes are rarely the ones who end up in the new development. I'd want strict conditions: proof no other site works, fair compensation well above market value, and a real community benefit requirement built into the deal, not just promised jobs that may not materialise. Without those safeguards I don't think projected tax revenue justifies taking someone's home.

commonMistakes: Not knowing what eminent domain means at all
Giving an absolute answer with no conditions or nuance
Ignoring the historical pattern of who eminent domain has displaced
followUps: How would you determine fair compensation beyond market price?

question: You're handed a six-lane arterial road lined with strip malls and parking lots, running through a mid-sized town. You have a modest budget and five years. What's your first move?
lookingFor: Practical, sequenced thinking about incremental transformation rather than a fantasy masterplan with no budget realism.

bullets: Start with data: traffic counts, pedestrian demand, crash history, and where transit already runs
Propose a phased, low-cost first step, such as road diet, protected bike lane, or a pilot pedestrian crossing, before big capital works
Tie the physical change to a land-use lever, like allowing mixed-use infill on the parking lots, since street design alone won't fix a dead corridor
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: With a modest budget I wouldn't start with a full redesign, I'd start with data on where people are actually crossing and getting hurt, because that tells me where a road diet would matter most, not just where it looks nice on a map. My first physical move would probably be a low-cost pilot, paint and planters to narrow the road and add a protected crossing, tested for six months before committing to concrete. But I'd pair that with a zoning change allowing mixed-use infill on those parking lots, because narrowing a road through a dead strip mall corridor won't create street life on its own, you need something for people to walk to.

commonMistakes: Proposing an expensive full rebuild that ignores the stated budget constraint
Only addressing the street design and ignoring the land-use side entirely
Skipping any data-gathering step and jumping straight to a design
followUps: How would you handle business owners who worry the road diet will hurt their parking access?

question: What makes transit-oriented development actually work, beyond just building housing near a train station?
lookingFor: Understanding that TOD is a design and policy bundle, not proximity alone.

bullets: Explain the density and mixed-use requirement around the station, usually within a walkable radius
Note the need for reduced or unbundled parking minimums so cars don't dominate the design anyway
Mention affordability and last-mile connectivity, since TOD near a station that's still unaffordable or hard to walk to fails its purpose
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Proximity to a station is necessary but not sufficient. What actually makes TOD work is pairing that proximity with enough density and mixed uses that people genuinely don't need a car for daily life, plus parking policy that doesn't undercut the whole point by requiring two spaces per unit anyway. I think the piece that gets missed most often is affordability, because if the transit access just gets capitalised into higher rents, you've built a nice amenity for people who could already afford a car, not the ridership base the transit line actually needs.

commonMistakes: Defining TOD as simply 'housing near a train station' with nothing more
Ignoring parking policy as part of the equation
Missing the affordability and displacement risk around new transit
followUps: How would you prevent transit-induced gentrification around a new station?

question: Some coastal towns are now considering 'managed retreat' rather than continuing to rebuild after repeated flooding. What is your view on this approach?
lookingFor: Awareness of a live, difficult planning debate and the ability to weigh community attachment against physical and financial risk.

bullets: Define managed retreat correctly: planned, funded relocation away from high-risk land rather than repeated rebuilding
Acknowledge the human cost: loss of community, identity, and place attachment, not just a technical relocation exercise
Discuss the alternative costs of not retreating, like repeated disaster funding and rising insurance failure, and land on a considered position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Managed retreat means planning and funding the relocation of a community away from land that keeps flooding, instead of rebuilding in place after every storm. I understand why it's controversial, because you're asking people to leave a place that holds their history, and that's not something a buyout cheque fully compensates for. But I've also read about towns where repeated federal disaster payouts cost more over a decade than relocation would have, and insurance markets are already pulling out of some of these areas anyway. I think the honest answer is that retreat has to be offered early and with real community input, not forced after the third flood when people have nothing left to negotiate with.

commonMistakes: Treating retreat as a purely technical or financial decision with no human cost
Being unaware the debate exists at all
Refusing to take any position on a genuinely difficult trade-off
followUps: Who should make this decision, the residents, the local government, or a national agency?

question: Should a city government prioritise upgrading informal settlements in place, or clearing them and rehousing residents elsewhere?
lookingFor: Awareness that in-situ upgrading is generally the evidence-backed approach, with reasoning for why, not just an assertion.

bullets: Show awareness that clearance historically destroys social and economic networks and often pushes people further from livelihoods
Explain the case for in-situ upgrading: incremental infrastructure, land tenure regularisation, keeping people near jobs and community
Acknowledge real exceptions, such as sites on unsafe land like floodplains or landslide zones, where relocation may genuinely be necessary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The evidence I've come across generally favours upgrading in place over clearance, because settlements like this usually sit close to jobs and have dense social networks that clearance destroys, often pushing people to the city edge where they lose both. In-situ upgrading, bringing in water, sanitation, and secure land tenure gradually, tends to improve conditions while respecting what residents have already built. That said, I don't think it's absolute, if a settlement sits on a floodplain or an unstable slope, relocation may genuinely be the safer answer, but even then it should be done with resident input and comparable access to livelihoods, not just moved out of sight.

commonMistakes: Defaulting to clearance as the obviously cleaner solution
Treating all informal settlements as identical regardless of site risk
Showing no awareness of tenure regularisation as a planning tool
followUps: What planning tools would you use to formalise land tenure in an informal settlement?

question: You run a community consultation for a new development, and the overwhelming resident feedback is opposed, but your analysis shows the project is genuinely needed and well designed. What do you do?
lookingFor: Ability to hold professional judgement and democratic legitimacy in tension rather than picking one and dismissing the other.

bullets: Take the opposition seriously rather than assuming residents just don't understand the benefits
Investigate whether the opposition reflects a real design flaw or an unaddressed concern, versus general resistance to change
Describe a path forward that involves revising the proposal or explaining trade-offs transparently, rather than either overriding residents or abandoning a needed project
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't assume the residents are simply wrong just because my analysis supports the project, because consultations that get ignored breed real distrust and often the opposition points to something the technical analysis missed, like construction disruption or a specific traffic concern. I'd go back through the feedback looking for patterns rather than treating it as one undifferentiated 'no', and see if the design can genuinely change to address the strongest objections. If after that the need is still clear and some opposition remains, I think the right move is to proceed with full transparency about the trade-offs and why the decision was made, rather than either steamrolling the community or shelving something the city actually needs.

commonMistakes: Dismissing resident opposition as simple NIMBYism without examining it
Abandoning a genuinely needed project purely to avoid conflict
Treating consultation as a box to check rather than input that can change the plan
followUps: What would make you conclude the opposition should actually stop the project?

question: Why did cities separate residential, commercial, and industrial land uses in the first place, and what's the case for undoing that today?
lookingFor: Historical grounding for Euclidean zoning plus a reasoned modern critique, not just repeating 'mixed-use good, separation bad'.

bullets: Explain the original public-health and nuisance rationale: separating housing from polluting factories and incompatible uses
Acknowledge that rationale made sense for heavy industry but was later applied far too broadly
Explain the modern case for mixed-use: walkability, economic vibrancy, reduced car dependence, more efficient land use
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Separated zoning came out of a real problem, early industrial cities put housing right next to polluting factories and slaughterhouses, and separating them was a genuine public-health win, which is what Euclid v. Ambler upheld. The issue is that the same logic got extended to separate ordinary shops and light offices from housing too, which doesn't have the same nuisance justification and just forces car trips for everything. The case for mixed-use today is that most modern commercial and light industrial activity isn't the hazard it was in 1920, so allowing a corner shop or a small office under an apartment building brings life back to a street without the original public-health risk that justified separation.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the historical public-health rationale behind zoning separation
Assuming all separation was always unjustified, ignoring legitimate heavy-industry cases
Giving a purely aesthetic argument for mixed-use with no functional reasoning
followUps: Are there uses today you'd still want kept separate from housing? Which, and why?

question: Congestion pricing schemes like New York's have been praised by planners but criticised as regressive. How would you respond to the equity criticism?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real current policy debate and the ability to engage with the equity critique honestly rather than dismissing it.

bullets: Show awareness of what congestion pricing is and a real example, and the stated goals: reduced traffic, cleaner air, transit funding
Take the regressivity critique seriously: lower-income drivers can be hit harder as a share of income, especially where transit alternatives are weak
Propose or discuss mitigations, such as revenue earmarked for transit improvements or discounts for lower-income drivers, rather than dismissing the concern
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know New York's congestion pricing scheme is meant to cut Manhattan traffic and fund transit upgrades with the toll revenue, and the early results on reduced congestion look genuinely promising. But I don't think the equity criticism should be waved away, a flat toll does take a bigger share of income from a lower-paid driver than a wealthy one, especially if their commute doesn't have a good transit alternative yet. I'd want the revenue transparently and quickly reinvested in the transit routes those same drivers could switch to, and I think discounted rates for low-income residents are worth exploring, because the policy only earns its legitimacy if the people paying the cost can see the benefit.

commonMistakes: Being unaware such schemes exist or have generated controversy
Dismissing the equity critique outright as anti-progress
Praising the policy with no acknowledgment of any downside
followUps: Should the toll rate vary by income, and how would you implement that fairly?

question: What causes the urban heat island effect, and what planning tools actually reduce it at the neighbourhood scale?
lookingFor: Technical grasp of the cause plus practical, specific interventions rather than a vague 'plant more trees' answer.

bullets: Explain the cause: dark impervious surfaces, lost vegetation, and waste heat from buildings and vehicles trapping heat
Name specific interventions: tree canopy targets, reflective or green roofs, permeable paving, reduced surface parking
Note that these tools need to be paired with equity awareness, since heat exposure is often worst in historically under-invested neighbourhoods
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The heat island effect happens because asphalt, concrete, and dark roofs absorb solar radiation and re-release it as heat instead of the evaporative cooling vegetation provides, and that gets compounded by waste heat from cars and air conditioning units. At neighbourhood scale I'd look at real tree canopy targets rather than token planting, reflective or green roofing requirements for new buildings, and converting some surface parking to permeable, shaded surfaces. What I find important is that heat exposure maps almost always overlap with historically redlined or under-invested neighbourhoods, so cooling interventions need to be targeted there first, not just wherever it's easiest to build.

commonMistakes: Giving only 'plant trees' with no other technical intervention
Not explaining the underlying physical cause at all
Missing the equity dimension of heat exposure entirely
followUps: How would you convince a budget-conscious council to fund a reflective roofing mandate?

question: A downtown plaza is used by skateboarders during the day and becomes a gathering spot for homeless residents at night, and nearby shopkeepers want it redesigned to discourage both. How would you approach the redesign?
lookingFor: Recognition of competing legitimate uses and skepticism toward hostile-design shortcuts, replaced with genuine problem-solving.

bullets: Identify that 'defensive' or hostile design, like spikes or segmented benches, displaces problems rather than solving them
Propose engaging all user groups, including skateboarders and outreach workers connected to homeless residents, not just the shopkeepers

Suggest a design and policy response that accommodates legitimate uses, such as a dedicated skate feature and connecting homeless residents to services, rather than simply removing people from the space
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My instinct is to resist the easy fix, hostile design like anti-skate ledges or armrests that block lying down doesn't solve anything, it just pushes the same people somewhere else, often somewhere worse. I'd want to actually talk to the skateboarders, since a plaza that draws them says something about a citywide lack of dedicated skate space, and to outreach workers who know the homeless residents using the plaza at night, because a redesign without a services response just relocates the problem. I'd bring the shopkeepers into that same conversation rather than treating their complaint as the only legitimate input, because a plaza that works for everyone is a better outcome for their businesses too than one that just displaces the visible symptom.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to hostile architecture as the solution
Only consulting the shopkeepers and ignoring the other user groups
Proposing to simply remove or police people out of the space with no alternative
followUps: What would you do if the council insisted on hostile design regardless of your advice?

question: Historic district designation protects neighbourhood character but is often criticised for blocking new housing supply. How do you weigh those two goods against each other?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with a real planning tension rather than declaring one value automatically superior.

bullets: Acknowledge the real value of preservation: cultural memory, architectural quality, community identity
Acknowledge the real cost: preservation districts can freeze supply in high-demand areas, worsening affordability city-wide
Propose a scoped approach, like limiting district size to genuinely significant blocks and allowing gentle infill or accessory units elsewhere, rather than an all-or-nothing stance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think this is a case where one value simply wins, historic character has real worth, it's part of how a city holds its own memory, but I've also read the research showing preservation districts in high-demand cities can meaningfully restrict housing supply and push up prices elsewhere. My approach would be to keep designation genuinely selective, reserved for blocks with real architectural or historical significance, rather than blanket protection over whole neighbourhoods because that's politically easier. And within a protected district I'd still look for ways to allow gentle density, like converting a single house to a duplex behind an unchanged facade, so preservation and housing supply aren't treated as strictly opposed.

commonMistakes: Treating preservation as sacred with no housing trade-off acknowledged
Dismissing preservation entirely as an obstacle to growth
Giving no concrete middle path, just naming the tension and stopping
followUps: Who should decide what counts as 'genuinely significant' enough to protect?

question: What went wrong with Sidewalk Labs' Quayside project in Toronto, and what does it tell you about 'smart city' planning?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real, well-known cautionary case and the ability to draw a genuine lesson from it.

bullets: Show basic awareness of the project: a Google-affiliated waterfront smart city proposal that was ultimately cancelled
Identify the core concerns that sank it: data governance and privacy questions, and public trust in a private company controlling civic data
Draw a lesson about planning: technology should serve a clear public governance framework, not be introduced faster than public trust or oversight can keep up
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sidewalk Labs proposed a heavily sensor-instrumented waterfront district in Toronto, and it eventually collapsed largely over data governance concerns, residents and officials didn't trust a private company controlling that much data about how people moved through a public neighbourhood, and it was never fully resolved before the project was scrapped. The lesson I take from it is that smart city technology has to follow public governance and consent, not lead it, a sensor network that makes planning more responsive is genuinely useful, but if residents don't know who owns the data or how it's used, the trust collapse undermines the whole project regardless of how good the technology is.

commonMistakes: No awareness of the case at all
Focusing only on technical features with no mention of the governance failure
Concluding smart city technology should never be used, missing the more nuanced governance lesson
followUps: How would you design a data governance framework you'd trust for a project like this?

question: Inclusionary zoning requires developers to include affordable units in new projects. Critics say it can actually reduce overall housing supply. Walk me through that argument.
lookingFor: Understanding of the economic mechanism behind the critique, not just familiarity with the policy's stated goal.

bullets: Explain the mechanism: mandates add cost to a project, which can make marginal developments unprofitable and get built less often or not at all
Explain the intended benefit it trades against: mixed-income buildings and affordable units delivered without direct public subsidy
Offer a considered view, such as design choices that soften the trade-off, like density bonuses offsetting the mandate cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The critique is essentially an economic one, if a mandate requires, say, twenty percent of units to be below-market rent, that cost has to come from somewhere, and in weaker markets it can push a project below the return a developer needs to build at all, so you end up with less total housing, market-rate and affordable both. The case for it is that it delivers affordable units without needing public subsidy dollars, which matters when budgets are tight. I think the honest answer is that it works best paired with a density bonus or fee waiver that offsets the added cost, so the developer isn't just absorbing a mandate, that's usually the difference between inclusionary zoning that gets projects built and one that quietly stalls them.

commonMistakes: Only stating the policy's goal without engaging with the supply critique
Dismissing the critique without understanding the underlying economics
Giving no view on how the trade-off might be softened
followUps: Would you set the affordability requirement as a fixed percentage or make it market-dependent?

question: You've been asked to design a new park for a low-income neighbourhood, but you know from other projects that new green space often raises nearby rents and pushes out the very residents it was meant to benefit. Do you still build it?
lookingFor: Willingness to hold a genuine ethical tension and propose real safeguards rather than either refusing outright or ignoring the risk.

bullets: Name the phenomenon accurately: green gentrification, where amenity investment raises land value and displaces existing residents
Refuse the false choice between 'no park' and 'ignore the risk', proposing protective policy alongside the physical project
Suggest concrete safeguards: rent stabilisation commitments, community land trusts, or anti-displacement zoning tied to the amenity investment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't take the easy way out and say don't build the park, because that punishes the neighbourhood twice, denying them the amenity because of a risk that's really a policy failure, not a park failure. What I'd push for is pairing the park with protections before it opens, rent stabilisation or property tax relief for long-term residents, maybe a community land trust for nearby housing, so the people who've lived there through the disinvested years are still there to enjoy the new investment. If the city won't commit to any of that alongside the park, I'd say so directly, because building green space without anti-displacement measures in a neighbourhood with this history is predictable, not accidental.

commonMistakes: Refusing to build the park as if withholding investment protects residents
Ignoring the displacement risk entirely and treating the park as an unqualified good
Naming the risk but proposing no concrete safeguard
followUps: What would you say if the council calls your safeguards too expensive to include?

question: What's the difference between comprehensive master planning and tactical urbanism, and when would you reach for each?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of both approaches and judgement about when incremental, low-cost testing beats a long-range plan.

bullets: Define master planning: a long-range, comprehensive document guiding land use and infrastructure over decades
Define tactical urbanism: low-cost, temporary, fast interventions like pop-up plazas or painted bike lanes used to test ideas
Give a clear rule for when each fits, such as tactical for testing contested or uncertain interventions quickly, master planning for setting long-term direction and legal zoning
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A master plan sets the long-range direction, land use, growth boundaries, infrastructure priorities over ten or twenty years, and it needs that horizon because zoning and capital projects take years to unfold. Tactical urbanism is almost the opposite, cheap, fast, and temporary, cones and paint to test a road diet or a plaza for a few weeks before committing real budget. I'd reach for tactical urbanism specifically when an idea is contested or unproven and I want real behavioural evidence before asking a council to spend capital funds, and I'd fold what works from that pilot back into the master plan rather than treating the two as separate tracks.

commonMistakes: Describing tactical urbanism as purely decorative with no strategic purpose
Treating the two as mutually exclusive rather than complementary
Vague or reversed definitions of the two terms
followUps: Give an example of a tactical pilot that you think should never become permanent.

question: You're assessing a former industrial site for redevelopment into housing. Soil tests show contamination that would cost a third of the project budget to fully remediate. What are your options, and how do you decide?
lookingFor: Technical and ethical awareness of remediation trade-offs, prioritising resident health over cost-cutting shortcuts.

bullets: Show awareness that remediation standards typically depend on end use, residential requiring stricter cleanup than commercial or industrial reuse
Weigh real options: full remediation, partial remediation with land-use restrictions, or reconsidering the site's intended use if housing isn't safely achievable within budget
Refuse to compromise on health and safety purely to protect project economics
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd check is what remediation standard actually applies for residential use, since contamination that's fine for commercial reuse often isn't safe enough for people living and children playing on that soil every day. If full residential-grade remediation blows the budget, I'd look at genuine alternatives before cutting corners, capping and paving contaminated areas as open space instead of building directly on them, or reconsidering whether this site is right for housing at all versus a commercial or light-industrial reuse that has a lower remediation bar. What I wouldn't do is push through partial remediation under a residential label just because the budget is tight, because that's a health decision being made on cost grounds, and that's not a trade-off I think a planner should make quietly.

commonMistakes: Proposing to skip or shortcut remediation to protect the budget
Not knowing that remediation standards vary by intended land use
Treating this as a purely financial decision with no health dimension
followUps: Who should bear the remediation cost, the developer, the city, or the original polluter if identifiable?

question: Many cities are eliminating minimum parking requirements. What's the planning logic behind that, and what's the strongest argument against it?
lookingFor: Understanding of parking minimums' hidden costs plus a fair-minded engagement with the opposing view.

bullets: Explain the case against minimums: they inflate construction costs, consume land that could be housing, and induce car dependence by guaranteeing free parking supply
Give the honest counter-argument: without minimums, street parking can get squeezed in areas with genuinely weak transit, frustrating existing residents
Show a reasoned view, such as removing minimums while investing in transit and managing on-street parking through pricing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The logic against parking minimums is that a fixed requirement, say two spaces per unit, forces developers to build parking whether or not residents want a car, and that land and construction cost gets baked into rents, plus guaranteed free-feeling parking just encourages more driving. The strongest argument against removing them is that in areas without decent transit yet, cutting the requirement can just push overflow onto already-tight street parking, which understandably frustrates existing residents. I'd support removing minimums, but I think it has to be sequenced with transit investment and smarter on-street pricing, otherwise you're solving a housing cost problem by creating a parking conflict.

commonMistakes: Only stating the pro-removal case with no acknowledgment of the counter-argument
Assuming eliminating minimums bans parking entirely, rather than making it optional
Giving no view on sequencing or transit as part of the answer
followUps: How would you manage on-street parking demand once minimums are removed?

subtopic: Remote work and downtown office vacancy
question: Downtown office vacancy has risen sharply in many cities since remote work became common. What planning responses have you seen proposed, and which do you think is most realistic?
lookingFor: Awareness of the current office-to-residential conversion debate and a grounded view of its practical limits.

bullets: Name the core proposed response: converting vacant office buildings to housing
Show awareness of the real technical barriers: floor plates too deep for natural light, plumbing and structural retrofit costs, zoning changes needed
Give a grounded view, such as conversion working well for some buildings and not others, and mention complementary responses like rezoning downtowns for mixed use
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The response I've read about most is converting vacant office towers to housing, but I think it's more limited than the headlines suggest, because a lot of office floor plates are too deep for units to get natural light without a costly structural overhaul, and older buildings often need entirely new plumbing risers to support apartments. It works well for narrower, older office stock, especially pre-1980s buildings, but not for the big glass floor-plate towers built for open-plan work. I think the more realistic citywide response is a mix, targeted conversions where the building type supports it, combined with rezoning downtowns for genuine mixed use so they don't empty out entirely outside office hours regardless of what happens to any single tower.

commonMistakes: Treating office-to-residential conversion as a universal, simple fix
No awareness of the technical retrofit barriers involved
Not knowing the underlying trend (remote work and vacancy) at all
followUps: What would you look for in a building to judge whether it's a good conversion candidate?

question: Your traffic model says a proposed pedestrian crossing isn't justified by the numbers, but residents insist it's a dangerous spot and keep asking for it. How do you reconcile the data with what residents are telling you?
lookingFor: Recognition that models have blind spots and lived experience is real evidence, not noise to be overridden by numbers.

bullets: Question the model's inputs and assumptions rather than treating the output as final truth, since traffic models can miss near-misses, informal crossing patterns, or vulnerable users like children and elderly residents
Treat resident testimony as a form of evidence worth investigating directly, not dismissing it as anecdotal
Propose a concrete next step, like a site observation or near-miss count, before deciding either way
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't treat the model's output as the final word, because standard crash-count models often miss near-misses and informal crossing behaviour that never shows up as a recorded collision, especially in spots where people cross exactly because there's no safe alternative nearby. I'd take the residents' concern seriously enough to actually go observe the intersection myself, at different times of day, and look specifically for who's crossing there and how close the calls are, particularly for children or elderly residents who might behave differently than the model's average pedestrian. If that observation backs up what residents are saying, I'd push for the crossing even against the raw numbers, because a model is a simplification, and residents living with the intersection every day are picking up on something real that the count missed.

commonMistakes: Deferring entirely to the model output and dismissing resident concern as anecdotal
Abandoning the data entirely just because residents are upset, with no independent verification
Proposing no concrete way to actually resolve the disagreement
followUps: What would make you conclude the residents were wrong and the model was right?

question: An elected official pressures you to approve a zoning variance for a campaign donor's project that your professional analysis says will overload local infrastructure. What do you do?
lookingFor: Firm professional and ethical boundaries under real pressure, expressed with realistic, non-naive judgement.

bullets: State clearly that professional analysis shouldn't be altered to fit political pressure, and explain why: public trust and safety, not just personal integrity
Describe a realistic response: document the technical findings clearly, put concerns in writing, escalate through proper channels rather than a quiet private confrontation
Acknowledge the real personal or career risk involved rather than pretending the choice is easy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't change my technical recommendation to fit the pressure, because if infrastructure genuinely can't support the project, approving it doesn't just breach my integrity, it creates real problems, overloaded sewage or traffic, for residents who had no say in the decision. What I'd actually do is put my findings in writing clearly and formally, so there's a documented record, and raise the pressure itself through whatever oversight or ethics channel exists rather than trying to resolve it quietly one-on-one with the official. I know that's not a comfortable position to be in, especially early in a career, but I think the alternative, quietly rubber-stamping decisions because of who's asking, is exactly how public trust in planning gets lost.

commonMistakes: Claiming the choice is easy with no acknowledgment of real professional risk
Suggesting they would simply comply to avoid conflict
Vague appeal to 'doing the right thing' with no concrete course of action
followUps: What would you do if your supervisor told you to approve it anyway?

question: What's lost when a city relies on privately owned public spaces, like a mall plaza or a corporate atrium, instead of genuinely public parks and squares?
lookingFor: Understanding of governance and access implications, not just aesthetic preference for public space.

bullets: Explain the core issue: privately owned spaces are governed by the owner's rules, not public rights, so access and speech can be restricted
Give a concrete consequence: protest, loitering, busking, or simply certain groups can be excluded at the owner's discretion
Balance it with the genuine reason cities use these spaces: they let dense development include public-feeling amenity without direct public capital cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The core issue is governance, a privately owned public space still looks and feels public, but it's the owner's rules that apply, not public rights, so things like protest, busking, or even just sitting too long can be restricted or enforced unevenly in ways a real city park can't be. That matters most for exactly the groups who most need accessible public space, since a mall management team can quietly exclude unhoused people or teenagers in ways a city council would face real accountability for. I understand why cities lean on these spaces, they let dense private development include plazas and seating without public capital, but I think that trade needs a binding public-access agreement attached, not just a handshake, or the city ends up with the appearance of public space without the substance of it.

commonMistakes: Treating privately owned public space as functionally identical to a real park
Focusing only on aesthetics rather than governance and access rights
Dismissing the practical reason cities rely on these spaces at all
followUps: What would a binding public-access agreement need to include to be meaningful?
